topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Electrolysis has appeared on the C2 paper every summer from 2023 to 2025, usually inside the aluminium question or as its own question of about ten marks, and the molten lead(II) bromide and lithium chloride cells were set in Unit 7 Chemistry Booklet B in Summer 2025. A half equation is [3] at Higher Tier.
mustMemorise: Electrolysis: the decomposition of a liquid electrolyte by a direct current
Electrolyte: conducts electricity and is decomposed by it
Inert electrode: takes no part in the reactions; graphite is inert, conducts electricity and has a high melting point
Molten: ions free to move and carry charge
Lead(II) bromide: lead (grey liquid) at the cathode, bromine (red-brown gas) at the anode
Lithium chloride: lithium (silvery-grey bead) at the cathode, chlorine (green gas) at the anode
Toxic gases (bromine, chlorine): use a fume cupboard
Cathode: ions gain electrons (reduction); anode: ions lose electrons (oxidation)

Relative atomic masses and group numbers (Chemistry Data Leaflet)
notOnThisSpec: Electrolysis of aqueous solutions and the discharge rules

Write the half equation at each electrode, including for the extraction of aluminium (Higher)

sheet.howExamined: C2: 1 hour 15 minutes, 70 marks at Foundation and 80 at Higher. Electrolysis appears most summers, often inside the aluminium question. Definitions are [1] to [2] and follow the glossary word for word in their key terms: 'decomposed', 'conducts', 'positive', 'negative'. Products and observations are [1] each. 'Why does the melt conduct' is [2]: the ions, free to move and carry charge. At Higher Tier a half equation is [3], awarded for the species with the arrow, then electrons on the correct side, then balancing, each dependent on the one before. Unit 7 Booklet B sets the same cells as apparatus: labelling the anode and naming the fume cupboard are marks.
traps: Naming electrons, not ions, as the particles that move and carry the charge in the melt (Summer 2023 C2 H Q3(a); Summer 2025 C2 H Q3(a))
Giving 'conducts' but not 'decomposed' in the definition of an electrolyte (Summer 2025 C2 F Q3(b); Summer 2023 C2 F Q3)
Writing 'a good conductor' for graphite without 'of electricity' (Summer 2023 C2 H Q3(b))
Naming bromide instead of bromine as the product at the anode, or not knowing it is a red-brown gas (Summer 2023 C2 H Q3(b); Summer 2025 C2 H Q3(b)(ii))
Defining the anode wrongly, or labelling a cell terminal instead of the electrode (Summer 2025 C2 H Q3(b)(i); Summer 2025 Unit 7 Chemistry Booklet B Q3)

noteBlocks.lede: Solid salt will not carry an electric current, but melt it and it will, and the current pulls the compound apart into its elements. That is electrolysis. This lesson follows the ions to the electrodes, names what forms at each one and what you see, and writes the reaction at each electrode.
can: Explain why a molten salt conducts and what electrolysis does to it.
Predict the product and the observation at each electrode for a molten salt.
Write the half equation at the anode and at the cathode (Higher).

noteBlocks.md: Push two graphite rods into solid lead(II) bromide, connect them to a battery, and nothing happens. Heat it until it melts and a current flows: a grey metal gathers under one rod and red-brown fumes rise from the other. The current is not simply passing through. It is taking the compound apart.

noteBlocks.caption: In the solid the ions are locked in place; in the melt they are free to move.

noteBlocks.md: An ionic compound is built from positive and negative **ions**. In the solid they are held in a lattice and cannot move, so no charge can flow. Melt it and the ions are **free to move**, so they **carry charge** through the liquid to the electrodes. That is why the compound must be **molten** (or dissolved).

noteBlocks.title: Why ions, not electrons
noteBlocks.md: Electrons carry the current in the wires and the rods, but there are no free electrons in a molten salt. In the melt the charge is carried by **ions** moving through the liquid. 'Free electrons' in the melt costs the mark every time.

noteBlocks.prompt: What carries the charge through molten lead(II) bromide?
noteBlocks.explain: Ions, moving through the liquid. Electrons only carry the current in the wires and the electrodes.

noteBlocks.md:
**Electrolysis** means using a direct electric current to **decompose** a liquid electrolyte: the compound is broken down, not just carried through.
**The electrolyte** is the molten or dissolved ionic compound. It **conducts** electricity **and is decomposed** as it does so.
**The anode** is the **positive** electrode; **the cathode** is the **negative** electrode.
An **inert electrode** takes no part in the reactions. Graphite is used because it is inert, **conducts electricity** and has a very high melting point.

noteBlocks.prompt: Complete the definition: an electrolyte conducts electricity and is ______ by it.
noteBlocks.answer: decomposed | broken down | decomposed by it
noteBlocks.explain: Decomposed. On a recent paper most candidates wrote 'conducts' and very few added 'decomposed', which is the second mark.

noteBlocks.prompt: An answer says graphite is used for electrodes because it is 'a good conductor'. Which two words must be added to earn the mark? (a good conductor of …)
noteBlocks.explain: 'A good conductor of electricity'. Examiners do not credit 'a good conductor' on its own, because it could mean heat.

noteBlocks.md:
One sentence predicts every product: **opposite charges attract**.
Metal ions are positive, so they move to the **negative cathode** and become metal atoms there. Non-metal ions are negative, so they move to the **positive anode** and become non-metal molecules.
So molten lithium chloride gives **lithium** at the cathode and **chlorine** at the anode. A check once you know the reason: **PANIC**, Positive is Anode, Negative Is Cathode.

noteBlocks.explain: Bromine. The negative bromide ions are attracted to the positive anode and leave as bromine, Br₂. Bromide is the ion you started with.

noteBlocks.md:
**The question.** Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed with graphite electrodes. Give the product and one observation at each electrode.
**Cathode.** Lead ions are attracted to it, so the product is **lead**. It forms as a **grey liquid**, because the crucible is hot enough to keep the lead molten.
**Anode.** Bromide ions are attracted to it, so the product is **bromine**: **bubbles of a red-brown gas**. Write *bromine*: bromide is the ion you started with.

noteBlocks.prompt: Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed. What is seen at the anode?
noteBlocks.explain: Bromine forms at the anode as a red-brown gas. The grey liquid is the lead, at the cathode.

noteBlocks.md:
A half equation shows what happens at one electrode. Build it in three steps.
**1.** Write the ion and the product. A non-metal leaves as a molecule: Br₂, Cl₂, O₂.
**2.** Balance the atoms, then compare the total charge on each side.
**3.** Add electrons, e⁻, to the side that needs them.
At the cathode ions **gain** electrons, so they sit on the left: $\ce{Pb^{2+} + 2e^- -> Pb}$. At the anode ions **lose** electrons, so they sit on the right: $\ce{2Br^- -> Br2 + 2e^-}$.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the anode half equation 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + ?e⁻, how many electrons are released?
noteBlocks.explain: Two. The left side carries −2 and the chlorine molecule carries 0, so two electrons go on the right to make the charges match.

noteBlocks.prompt: Molten lithium chloride is electrolysed. Which is the half equation at the cathode?
noteBlocks.explain: At the cathode the positive ion gains an electron, so the electron goes in on the left: +1 − 1 = 0 on each side.

noteBlocks.md:
The same method works for any molten compound of a metal and a non-metal. Magnesium chloride gives magnesium, $\ce{Mg^{2+} + 2e^- -> Mg}$, and chlorine.
Aluminium is extracted by electrolysing aluminium oxide: $\ce{Al^{3+} + 3e^- -> Al}$ at the cathode and $\ce{2O^{2-} -> O2 + 4e^-}$ at the anode. Oxygen leaves as O₂, so two oxide ions are needed, and together they lose four electrons.

noteBlocks.prompt: At the anode in aluminium extraction, 2O²⁻ → O₂ + ?e⁻. How many electrons are released?
noteBlocks.explain: Four. Two oxide ions carry −2 each, −4 in all, and the oxygen molecule carries 0, so four electrons go on the right.

noteBlocks.md: The two half equations are the two halves of a redox reaction. Gaining electrons is **reduction**, so the cathode reaction is always a reduction; losing electrons is **oxidation**, so the anode reaction is always an oxidation.

noteBlocks.prompt: At the cathode, Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb. What happens to the lead ions?

they are oxidised, because they gain electrons
they are reduced, because they lose electrons

noteBlocks.explain: Reduction Is Gain of electrons. The anode reaction, where bromide ions lose electrons, is the oxidation.

parts.stem:
Molten sodium chloride can be electrolysed using graphite electrodes.
Describe and explain what happens. Include why the sodium chloride must be molten, what happens at each electrode, what would be seen, and one safety precaution.
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

indicativeContent.point: sodium chloride is made of ions: positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions
when molten the ions are free to move and carry charge
positive sodium ions are attracted to the negative cathode
at the cathode the sodium ions gain electrons and form sodium metal
negative chloride ions are attracted to the positive anode
at the anode the chloride ions lose electrons and form chlorine gas
bubbles of a green gas are seen at the anode and a silvery liquid metal at the cathode

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Start with the particles: what is sodium chloride made of, and why must it melt?
Then take each electrode in turn: which ion, what it does with electrons, what forms, what you see.
Finish with the safety point, naming the gas.
parts.workedSolution: Sodium chloride is made of positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions. When it is molten the ions are free to move, so they can carry charge through the liquid. The positive sodium ions are attracted to the negative cathode, where each gains an electron and becomes sodium metal, seen as a silvery liquid. The negative chloride ions are attracted to the positive anode, where they lose electrons and form chlorine gas, seen as bubbles of a green gas. Graphite is used for the electrodes because it is inert and conducts electricity. Chlorine is toxic, so the electrolysis is carried out in a fume cupboard.

commonErrors.feedback: Check the sentence about what moves through the melt: it is the ions, not electrons. Summer 2025 examiners found this error in many extraction answers.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ethan is asked: 'Write the half equation at the anode when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. [3]'
He sets out his answer in steps:
studentWorking: ion attracted to the anode = Cl⁻
product formed at the anode = Cl
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right: the negative chloride ions go to the positive anode. Line 2 writes the product as a single atom, but chlorine exists as molecules, Cl₂. Everything after that is built on the atom, so the half equation in line 3 is wrong too, although the electron is on the correct side. Summer 2025 Unit 7 examiners found the anode half equation the hardest part of the lithium chloride question.
correction: product formed at the anode = Cl₂
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks as written: the first mark needs the right ion and product with an arrow, and each later mark depends on it. Write the molecule first, Cl₂, then balance the chloride ions to it, then add the electrons.

findTheMistake.stem:
Aoife is asked: 'Molten lead(II) bromide is electrolysed. Name the product at each electrode and give one observation at each. [4]'
Her answer:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Bromide is the ion that arrives at the anode. There the ions lose electrons and become bromine, the element, which is the product. Her observation in line 4 is exactly right, and it describes bromine, not bromide: bromide ions are colourless. Summer 2023 examiners found many candidates gave bromide as the product at the anode.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three of the four marks. The product at the anode is the one that goes. The rule: an -ide name is an ion in a compound; what forms at the anode is the element, with an -ine name.

findTheMistake.stem:
Conor is asked: 'Write the half equation at the cathode in the extraction of aluminium. [3]'
He sets out his answer in steps:
studentWorking: ion attracted to the cathode = Al³⁺
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right. Line 2 is where it slips: an Al³⁺ ion carries three positive charges, so it needs three electrons to become a neutral atom. With only two, the left side carries +3 − 2 = +1 while the right carries 0. The electrons are on the correct side in line 3; only the number is wrong.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks: the ion and product with an arrow, and the electrons on the correct side. The balancing mark goes. Count the charge on each side before you finish: they must be equal.

prompts.prompt: Write the half equation at the cathode for molten lead(II) bromide.

prompts.prompt: Write the half equation at the anode for molten lead(II) bromide.

findings.asked: Name the particle that moves and carries the charge in a molten electrolyte, say what happens to the electrolyte, and give the products, observations and a half equation for molten lead(II) bromide.
findings.wentWrong: Very few identified an ion as the moving charged particle; only some said the electrolyte decomposes; 'a good conductor' was written without 'of electricity'; many named bromide as the product at the anode; and the half equation lacked the bromine molecule or had its electrons on the wrong side.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Named ions as the charge carriers, said the electrolyte is decomposed, gave 'conductor of electricity', and wrote bromine, a red-brown gas, at the anode.
findings.rule: Ions carry the charge in the melt; an -ide is the ion, an -ine is the element that forms.

findings.asked: Explain why a molten ionic compound conducts, and write the half equation for oxygen forming at the anode.
findings.wentWrong: Many wrote about free electrons in the melt, or ions carrying current or electricity, and neither was credited. Few wrote the anode half equation correctly: the commonest fault was forming an oxygen atom instead of the molecule.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Said the ions are free to move and carry charge, and wrote 2O²⁻ → O₂ + 4e⁻, earning a mark each for the species with the arrow, the electrons on the correct side and the balancing, in that order.
findings.rule: Ions carry charge, not current. Write the molecule first in any half equation that makes a gas.

findings.asked: Complete the definition of an electrolyte.
findings.wentWrong: Many gained the mark for 'conducts' but few gained the second mark for 'decomposed' or 'broken down'.
findings.rule: An electrolyte conducts electricity and is decomposed by it: two ideas, two marks.

findings.asked: Define the term anode, and identify the element that bubbles off the anode as a red-brown gas when a lithium halide is electrolysed.
findings.wentWrong: Only about half could define the anode, and very few identified bromine as the red-brown gas.
findings.rule: The anode is the positive electrode. Red-brown at the anode means bromine.

findings.asked: Label the anode on a diagram of the molten lead(II) bromide apparatus, say where the experiment should be done, and describe what is seen at the anode.
findings.wentWrong: The anode label was poorly answered, with cell terminals labelled or the electrodes confused; the safety answers were general rather than specific to a toxic gas; and many did not know bromine's colour or wrote bromide.
findings.rule: Follow the wire to the positive terminal to find the anode; toxic gas means fume cupboard; bromine is red-brown.

findings.asked: Fill in a table for molten lithium chloride: what is seen, what forms and the half equation at each electrode.
findings.wentWrong: Most completed the table correctly; the balanced half equation at the anode was the part candidates found hardest.
findings.rule: At the anode: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. Two chloride ions for one chlorine molecule, electrons on the right.

insight.ruleToRemember: Opposite charges attract: metal at the negative cathode, non-metal at the positive anode. Ions carry the charge in the melt. Name the element that forms (bromine, not bromide), give its colour and that it is a gas, and write half equations from the molecule, with the electrons wherever they make the charges equal.
insight.aStarSignal: A half equation that starts from the diatomic molecule and puts the electrons on the side the charges demand, with the electrode named as the site of reduction or oxidation.
